In [[mathematics]], the '''Morse–Palais lemma''' is a result in the [[calculus of variations]] and theory of [[Hilbert spaces]]. Roughly speaking, it states that a [[Smooth function|smooth]] enough [[Function (mathematics)|function]] near a critical point can be expressed as a [[quadratic form]] after a suitable change of coordinates.

The Morse–Palais lemma was originally proved in the finite-dimensional case by the [[United States|American]] [[mathematician]] [[Marston Morse]], using the [[Gram–Schmidt process|Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization process]]. This result plays a crucial role in [[Morse theory]].  The generalization to Hilbert spaces is due to [[Richard Palais]] and [[Stephen Smale]].

== Statement of the lemma ==

Let <math>(H, \langle \cdot ,\cdot \rangle)</math> be a [[Real number|real]] Hilbert space, and let <math>U</math> be an [[Open set|open neighbourhood]] of the origin in <math>H.</math> Let <math>f : U \to \R</math> be a <math>(k+2)</math>-times continuously [[differentiable function]] with <math>k \geq 1;</math> that is, <math>f \in C^{k+2}(U; \R).</math> Assume that <math>f(0) = 0</math> and that <math>0</math> is a non-degenerate [[Critical point (mathematics)|critical point]] of <math>f;</math> that is, the second derivative <math>D^2 f(0)</math> defines an [[isomorphism]] of <math>H</math> with its [[continuous dual space]] <math>H^*</math> by
<math display=block>H \ni x \mapsto \mathrm{D}^2 f(0) (x, -) \in H^*.</math>

Then there exists a subneighbourhood <math>V</math> of <math>0</math> in <math>U,</math> a [[diffeomorphism]] <math>\varphi : V \to V</math> that is <math>C^k</math> with <math>C^k</math> inverse, and an [[Invertible function|invertible]] [[symmetric operator]] <math>A : H \to H,</math> such that
<math display=block>f(x) = \langle A \varphi(x), \varphi(x) \rangle \quad \text{ for all } x \in V.</math>

== Corollary ==

Let <math>f : U \to \R</math> be <math>f \in C^{k+2}</math> such that <math>0</math> is a non-degenerate critical point. Then there exists a <math>C^k</math>-with-<math>C^k</math>-inverse diffeomorphism <math>\psi : V \to V</math> and an [[orthogonal decomposition]]
<math display=block>H = G \oplus G^{\perp},</math>
such that, if one writes
<math display=block>\psi (x) = y + z \quad \mbox{ with } y \in G, z \in G^{\perp},</math>
then
<math display=block>f (\psi(x)) = \langle y, y \rangle - \langle z, z \rangle \quad \text{ for all } x \in V.</math>
